title: Ramadan: the iftar cannon
hookLine: in some cities a cannon marks sunset for breaking the fast

lines: THE WHOLE HOUSE MOVES AT ONCE.
cards: Late afternoon in the fasting month. A table is laid: dates in a bowl, water in glasses, soup keeping warm, a plate nobody may touch yet. Children hover.
Somebody checks the window; somebody else checks a phone. Everyone is listening. Then, from the hill across the city, a deep boom rolls over the rooftops, and the whole house moves at once.
A date. A sip of water. Someone laughs.
In some cities, that boom is the sound of sunset in Ramadan. Today: the iftar cannon.

teach.h: STRICTLY OBSERVE THE FAST TILL NIGHTFALL.
teach.b: First, what the cannon answers. The Qur'an sets the edges of the fasting day: eat and drink until the dawn is clear, and then, in Pickthall's translation, "Then strictly observe the fast till nightfall."
In Sunni practice the fast ends at sunset, with the call to the sunset prayer; in Shia practice, a little later, when the redness has left the eastern sky.
Before clocks on every wrist, a whole city needed to know the same moment. A call from a minaret carries only so far; a cannon carries much farther. Second, the story.

teach.h: A CANNON FIRED BY CHANCE, THEY SAY.
teach.b: People in Cairo tell it in several versions: a ruler was testing a new cannon, and by chance it fired just at sunset in Ramadan. The people took it as a signal and thanked him, and the firing became a custom.
Whether it happened that way, nobody can say. But the custom spread, and in some cities a cannon still fires at sunset in Ramadan, sometimes carried on television and radio. Third, the hurry.
A hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari says people will remain in good as long as they hurry to break the fast. Not lingering, not proving how long you can last.
The Qur'an gives the fast a firm edge at both ends, and the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, asked people not to blur the second. Fourth, the joy.

teach.h: TWO JOYS FOR THE ONE WHO FASTS.
teach.b: Another hadith says the one who fasts has two joys: one when breaking the fast, and one on meeting the Lord.
The cannon is the sound of the first joy, heard by a whole city at once.

how: Muslims fasting in Ramadan break the fast at the call to the maghrib prayer, at sunset or, in Shia practice, a little after, often with dates and water; in some cities a cannon is fired at that moment.

s: the Qur'an commands a cannon at sunset
the Qur'an sets the fast till nightfall. the cannon is a later custom, with a story people tell about its start.
a hadith praises hurrying to break the fast
people will remain in good as long as they hurry to break the fast.

games.q: you're fasting. the sun is down and the call to the sunset prayer has sounded, but you feel strong. what does the hadith encourage?
o: keep fasting a while longer, to show your strength.
wait until after the night prayer.
games.why: the hadith says people remain in good as long as they hurry to break the fast. the fast has a firm edge at both ends.

practice: Listen to whatever sounds are around you, traffic, a fridge, a bird, your own breath, and simply wait, the way a family waits at the table. When the bell comes, let it be your cannon: take one slow sip of water and notice it.
If you're fasting today, let this remind you to break the fast on time; if you pray, give thanks in the words you know.

wordCard.voice: Ramadan. The month of fasting from dawn to nightfall, and in some cities, the month a cannon tells everyone at once that the sun is down. Today's word.
